This page discusses the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore's (MPA) cybersecurity tabletop exercises aimed at improving port resilience through business continuity planning. The exercises involve international participants and simulate cyberattacks across multiple ports, testing coordination mechanisms under different regulatory frameworks. It emphasizes the importance of considering cyber risks alongside physical risks and suggests backup strategies for recovery.

This page discusses the enforcement and oversight of cybersecurity regulations in ports, highlighting various national frameworks and their implementation. It emphasizes the differences in institutional capacity and regulatory maturity across countries, with examples from Japan, Singapore, and the EU. The text also notes the uneven development of cybersecurity governance, with statistics on countries having national strategies and agencies, and the impact of legal instruments on compliance and enforcement.

Selected recommendations:

•   Training: Implement role-based, recurrent cybersecurity training across all staff levels, covering
   both IT and OT threat scenarios.

•   Culture: Foster a no-blame reporting culture that treats incident disclosure as a contribution to
    collective defense rather than an admission of failure.

•   Incentives: Treat cyber-resilient supply chains as a public good and reflect this in governance
   frameworks and contractual arrangements. For example, invest in cyber resilience centers
   and cross-sector capacity building to enhance coordinated detection, intelligence sharing, and
    incident response capabilities.

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                              55



Ports sit at the center of modern economies and supply chains—and increasingly at the center of
modern cyber risk. As the sector shifts toward “Port 4.0” operations, integrates port community
systems and electronic Maritime Single Windows, and links information technologies with
operational technologies (IT with OT), cyber incidents no longer threaten only data or office systems.
They can halt vessel movements and port operations, disrupt national trade flows, create safety
risks, and propagate across the port ecosystem and beyond. In this context, cyber resilience has
become inseparable from operational resilience.

At the same time, strengthening cybersecurity does not necessarily require the creation of entirely
new institutional structures. Many of the capabilities needed to improve cyber resilience already
exist within port governance and operational practices. Ports routinely manage operational
risks, oversee third-party vendors, conduct training programs, maintain busine

relevant to operational technology (also called industrial control systems) and an overview of

2.1 Evaluating Risk: Knowing What You Are Up Against

2.1.1 How Do Incidents Occur?

Understanding how incidents enter port systems is a prerequisite for protecting them. The
overwhelming majority of port cyber incidents documented in the literature involve the exploitation
of well-known, preventable weaknesses rather than novel techniques (Meland et al. 2021; Chubb et
al. 2022; Badea et al. 2025). This has important implications: for most ports, basic and consistent
implementation of established protective controls would materially reduce exposure of information
and operational technologies (IT and OT).

points to several recurring entry points in port environments:

•   phishing and social engineering targeting staff,

•   exploitation of unpatched software vulnerabilities in IT systems,

•   insecure or unmonitored remote access connections,

question: In Figure 5, list the four port governance models top-to-bottom and explain how public and private responsibility change from the top model to the bottom.
answer: The four port governance models, from top to bottom, are Public Service Port, Tool Port, Landlord Port, and Private Port. In the Public Service Port model, public responsibility is primary and private responsibility is limited. As it transitions to the Tool Port and then the Landlord Port, public responsibility decreases while private responsibility increases. In the Private Port model, private responsibility is primary and public responsibility is limited.

2.3 Main Takeaways and Key Recommendations

Many ports struggle to maintain a current risk picture and implement security controls into
routine operations across IT/OT. At the same time, incident readiness remains under-practiced and
insufficiently integrated with business continuity. A central challenge of cybersecurity in ports is
the transition from one-off risk-gauging efforts to continuous outcomes-focused risk management
(IMO 2025). By integrating cybersecurity responsibilities into established processes, such as risk
management, operations oversight, business continuity planning, and procurement, ports can
strengthen resilience without creating parallel institutional frameworks.

Further Resources to Improve Protection.

In high-income settings, almost 69 percent of respondents conduct vulnerability scans or more
specific penetration tests at least annually, and nearly a third do so every three months or more
(Figure 8). In middle-income countries, this proportion falls to approximately half of the respondents.
By contrast, half of the respondents from low-income countries conduct vulnerability scans
less than once a year or never. The absence of routine scanning and testing leaves weaknesses
unaddressed and increases the likelihood that attempted intrusions with widely available malicious
software will succeed (NIST 2022).

The World Bank survey indicates that recent cybersecurity risk assessments are more prevalent in high-income countries compared to low- and middle-income countries. Among high-income respondents, 79% reported conducting such assessments in the past 24 months, while the figures drop significantly in lower-income contexts. This disparity is attributed to the varying maturity levels of legal requirements across different income categories.

This page discusses national approaches to integrating cybersecurity into ISPS-based port security frameworks, highlighting the Italian Coast Guard's Circular No. 177/2025 and Chile's Circular O 75/006. Both frameworks emphasize the importance of incorporating cybersecurity considerations into existing security and risk management practices for port facilities. They require assessments of cyber threats, updates to security plans, and the designation of cybersecurity officers to manage risks effectively.

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                                            11



In the absence of binding global cybersecurity requirements for ports, some countries have adapted
existing maritime security frameworks—most notably those derived from the ISPS Code—to
incorporate explicit cybersecurity obligations at the national level, as illustrated in Box 4.


    Box 4 Case studies: National approaches to integrating cybersecurity into
    ISPS‑based port security frameworks

    The Navigation Safety – General Series Circular No. 177/2025, issued by the Italian Coast
     Guard, provides operational guidance on integrating cyber-risk management into the
     maritime sector, with specific implications for port authorities and port facilities. While
     the circular applies more broadly to ships and shipping companies, it requires port facilities
     to explicitly incorporate cybersecurity considerations into their existing security and risk
    management frameworks. In practice, port facilities must assess cyber threats as part of

es
     to explicitly incorporate cybersecurity considerations into their existing security and risk
    management frameworks. In practice, port facilities must assess cyber threats as part of
      their security assessments, update Port Facility Security Plans accordingly, and ensure the
     protection of critical digital systems used in port operations, including logistics platforms,
    communications networks, access-control systems, and other operational infrastructure.
    To avoid regulatory duplication, the circular exempts port facilities already covered by
     the European Union Directive on Network and Information Systems (NIS2) from additional
     requirements. It also emphasizes staff training, cyber-incident prevention and response
     procedures, and alignment with international guidance issued by the IMO and the European
     cybersecurity framework established under NIS2, recognizing cybersecurity as an integral
    component of port infrastructure security.

    A comparable approach has been adopted in Chile through Circular O 75/006, issued

At an operational level, these systemic risks are shaped by the increasing integration of information
technology (IT) and operational technology (OT) within port environments. Modern ports operate
complex, networked systems in which IT applications—traditionally used for data management,
commercial records, and administrative processes—are closely linked to OT systems that control
physical operations such as cargo handling, crane and conveyor movements, and energy and facility
management (Lagouvardou 2018; Li et al. 2024). This convergence is significant because IT and OT
systems have distinct security requirements and risk tolerances, and failures can affect ports in
fundamentally different ways. While cyber incidents2 affecting IT systems typically disrupt data
integrity, financial transactions, or administrative operations, incidents involving OT systems
can halt cargo movement, damage physical assets, and, in severe cases, endanger human safety.

collective action. These barriers are mutually reinforcing, and addressing any one of them in isolation

This page provides an overview of the Return on Security Investment (ROSI) calculation, detailing key inputs such as Single Loss Expectancy (SLE), Annual Rate of Occurrence (ARO), and Annual Loss Expectancy (ALE). It outlines the core calculation for ROSI and practical steps for quantifying baseline risk, estimating control mitigation rates, and performing sensitivity analysis. Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                                44




    Box 10 Return on Security Investment (ROSI) calculation overview

    ROSI quantifies the economic value of a security control by estimating the avoided losses
      relative to the control’s cost. It adapts the classic return-on-investment (ROI) approach to a
     loss-prevention context, answering whether a given security expenditure is cost-effective.

    Key inputs:

      •   Single Loss Expectancy (SLE): estimated monetary loss per incident (includes direct and
          indirect impacts).

      •   Annual Rate of Occurrence (ARO): expected frequency of incidents per year.

      •   Annual Loss Expectancy (ALE): SLE × ARO. This is the baseline risk exposure.

      •   Control efficacy (mitigation rate): proportion by which the control reduces ALE.

      •   Total cost of control: acquisition, implementation, operations.

    Core calculation:

      •  ROSI = [(ALE × mitigation rate) – cost of control] / cost of control

     Practical steps:

      •   Quantify baseline risk (SLE, ARO) for specific threat-asset pairs.

      •   Estimate the control’s mitigation rate (evidence from pilots, audits, and incident data).

      •   Include full life-cycle costs (tools, integration, staffing).

    Box 10 Return on Security Investment (ROSI) calculation overview

    ROSI quantifies the economic value of a security control by estimating the avoided losses
      relative to the control’s cost. It adapts the classic return-on-investment (ROI) approach to a
     loss-prevention context, answering whether a given security expenditure is cost-effective.

    Core calculation:

      •  ROSI = [(ALE × mitigation rate) – cost of control] / cost of control

This page provides an overview of the Return on Security Investment (ROSI) calculation, detailing key inputs such as Single Loss Expectancy (SLE), Annual Rate of Occurrence (ARO), and Annual Loss Expectancy (ALE). It outlines the core calculation for ROSI and practical steps for quantifying baseline risk, estimating control mitigation rates, and performing sensitivity analysis. The page emphasizes that ROSI should be used as a decision support tool within a broader risk assessment framework.

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                                44




    Box 10 Return on Security Investment (ROSI) calculation overview

    ROSI quantifies the economic value of a security control by estimating the avoided losses
      relative to the control’s cost. It adapts the classic return-on-investment (ROI) approach to a
     loss-prevention context, answering whether a given security expenditure is cost-effective.

    Key inputs:

      •   Single Loss Expectancy (SLE): estimated monetary loss per incident (includes direct and
          indirect impacts).

      •   Annual Rate of Occurrence (ARO): expected frequency of incidents per year.

      •   Annual Loss Expectancy (ALE): SLE × ARO. This is the baseline risk exposure.

      •   Control efficacy (mitigation rate): proportion by which the control reduces ALE.

      •   Total cost of control: acquisition, implementation, operations.

    Core calculation:

      •  ROSI = [(ALE × mitigation rate) – cost of control] / cost of control

that investments are strategically allocated for them to translate into meaningful protection,
while remaining aligned with the organization’s financial sustainability objectives (Carfora and

    Core calculation:

      •  ROSI = [(ALE × mitigation rate) – cost of control] / cost of control

      •   Interpreting results: >0 indicates net savings; higher values indicate better cost-
         effectiveness. Use ranges for uncertainty.

     Practical steps:

      •   Quantify baseline risk (SLE, ARO) for specific threat-asset pairs.

      •   Estimate the control’s mitigation rate (evidence from pilots, audits, and incident data).

      •   Include full life-cycle costs (tools, integration, staffing).

      •   Perform sensitivity analysis (best/base/worst case scenarios) and revisit annually.

    Outputs should be treated as decision support tools and not forecasts, as precise impact
     estimation is difficult. ROSI should still be used within a broader quantitative
      risk assessment, pairing financial estimates with operational metrics and
     periodic reviews to keep decisions on cybersecurity investment evidence-based.

Addressing these vulnerabilities is difficult in OT environments where downtime is operationally
costly, but important to maintaining port security and competitiveness. This can be done through
mandatory refresh cycles for software and physical infrastructure housing the IT systems. Where
replacement is impractical, controls that compensate for known vulnerabilities of these legacy
systems should be implemented. Network segmentation, discussed in Box 6, is one possible effective

    Many OT networks in ports were originally designed as closed, air-gapped systems. As

Cybersecurity in Ports: Shifting from Risk to Resilience                                               3



At an operational level, these systemic risks are shaped by the increasing integration of information
technology (IT) and operational technology (OT) within port environments. Modern ports operate
complex, networked systems in which IT applications—traditionally used for data management,
commercial records, and administrative processes—are closely linked to OT systems that control
physical operations such as cargo handling, crane and conveyor movements, and energy and facility
management (Lagouvardou 2018; Li et al. 2024). This convergence is significant because IT and OT
systems have distinct security requirements and risk tolerances, and failures can affect ports in
fundamentally different ways. While cyber incidents2 affecting IT systems typically disrupt data
integrity, financial transactions, or administrative operations, incidents involving OT systems
can halt cargo movement, damage physical assets, and, in severe cases, endanger human safety.

represented a geographically diverse set of organizations across Europe and Central Asia; East Asia
and the Pacific; the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan; North America; Sub-Saharan

This page discusses the economic and employment impacts of cyber incidents in maritime transport, highlighting potential losses exceeding $100 billion in the Asia-Pacific region and significant costs in the U.S. It emphasizes the importance of cybersecurity for job stability and creation in ports, noting the growing demand for specialized cybersecurity roles. The page also addresses cybersecurity as a development challenge, pointing out disparities in cybersecurity capacity between low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and high-income countries, with LMICs scoring lower on the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index. This disparity has macroeconomic implications, potentially reducing GDP per capita by about 1.5 percent in LMICs.

pandemic—have demonstrated the sensitivity of maritime transport networks to systemic
disruptions, with measurable contractions in seaborne trade (Idrees et al. 2025). Cyber incidents can
generate similar cascading effects, as operational disruptions in one port propagate through tightly
coupled supply chains. Economic modeling suggests that a severe cyber incident affecting major
ports could generate losses exceeding $100 billion in the Asia-Pacific region alone (Lloyd’s List 2019),
while the prolonged shutdown of a single major U.S. port could cost its regional economy billions per
month (Varley et al. 2024). Already in 2023, the average cost of a cyber incident in the maritime
transport sector reached $550,000, a threefold increase from 2022, and ransom demands averaged
$3.2 million (Kenney and Macdonald 2023).

This page discusses the importance of specialized training and professional development in cybersecurity for port employees. It highlights the effectiveness of tailored training programs over generic ones, emphasizing the need for role-specific content. The page includes Figure 13, which contrasts 'One size fits all' cybersecurity training with 'Personalized cybersecurity training' for different port roles. Survey results indicate disparities in training availability, with high-income countries more likely to provide annual specialized training compared to lower-middle and low-income countries. The lack of investment in technical capacity development is noted as a concern in LMICs, with Box 9 referenced for best-practice examples.

This page presents Figure 12, which illustrates the provision of regular cybersecurity awareness training for employees across different income levels. The data highlights the percentage of responses regarding whether organizations provide training, with categories including 'Yes, at least once a year,' 'Yes, but less than once a year,' 'No, no formal training is provided,' and 'Prefer not to say.' The figure emphasizes the importance of training in mitigating cybersecurity vulnerabilities identified by interviewees.

skills form the backbone of organizations’ defensive capabilities. A key theme that emerged across
multiple interviews and the literature was the critical importance of tailoring training to specific
roles rather than deploying only generic content (Oruc et al. 2024), as illustrated in Figure 13.

a critical challenge: a large share of incidents can be traced to unintentional insiders with limited

This section discusses aligning economic incentives to enhance cyber resilience in ports. It emphasizes the importance of linking cybersecurity investments to incentives through concession agreements, cost-sharing mechanisms, and clear liability rules. The text highlights the need for cooperation among port authorities and operators to address economic misalignment and promote shared cybersecurity efforts. It also outlines the role of governments and private operators in improving cybersecurity through regulatory measures and contractual obligations, ultimately aiming to align private incentives with collective resilience goals.

Effective cybersecurity in ports depends on local governance arrangements that define

model under which a port operates (IAPH 2021). Different governance systems—such as public
service, tool, landlord, and fully private models—determine how ownership, operational control, and
risk management responsibilities are distributed across the port community (World Bank 2025b).
